items.content:
Despite US-Israeli airstrikes and Tehran’s attacks on shipping, the waterway still has to provide a lifeline for those that live and work there
By Stefanie Glinski ; photographs by Mohammad Mohsenifar in Bandar Abbas/on Hormuz Island
Capt Farouq turns the wheel as he watches the ferry terminal of Bandar Abbas grow smaller, its bright lights flickering in the distance.
In front of him, the navigation radar beeps periodically, its green and pink lights glowing in the darkness. The ferry, today at about half capacity with roughly 100 passengers, turns and heads into the darkness of the strait of Hormuz.
He’s been a captain for the past 18 years, and the strait of Hormuz is his second home
Farouq, 39, sits comfortably in his cabin, overlooking the pitch black horizon as he sails towards Hormuz Island, a short commute of about half an hour from the Iranian mainland’s Haqqani Port, for 340,000 toman, about £1. He is relaxed and smiles as he pulls into the deeper waters. He’s been a captain for the past 18 years, and the strait of Hormuz is his second home.
Farouq says the crossings have not stopped since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran on 28 February, although passenger numbers are down and the journey has become more dangerous. For months, Farouq has heard explosions coming from the strait, unclear as to whether that is air defence or attacks, or both. Tonight is no different.
Inside the ferry, passengers say they have gotten used to the sounds too, and, to an extent, the war itself. They drink tea and smoke cigarettes. Some nap, while others entertain their children. It’s hot and humid, the air thick, the windows fogged with condensation.
Even with a fragile ceasefire in place, here on the coast, it has barely felt as though the war has stopped.
According to Iranian government sources, attacks on the southern port of Bandar Abbas have damaged 760 fishing and commercial vessels. Farouq says his own ferry was also damaged by shrapnel while docked at the port, though it was quickly repaired.
Since the start of the war, Iranian forces have repeatedly attacked vessels attempting to cross the strait. In the first week of October alone, at least 12 attacks were reported against oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers, sending oil prices back above $100 a barrel .
With pressure mounting on the US president, Donald Trump, before the midterm elections, he is rumoured to be once again considering strikes.
But beyond the headlines and global markets, the strait is first and foremost a lifeline for many Iranians living in the southern province of Hormozgan.
Fishers in Bandar Abbas selling their catch on the street
Fishers, captains and harbour workers all depend on the strait for their livelihoods and the war has made their work increasingly difficult. Fishers can no longer venture as far out, ports have come under attack, and many people fled Bandar Abbas in the early months of the war for smaller, more remote villages in search of safety.
Local residents fishing for their own daily consumption
Anvar Sadat, a 38-year-old fisher who works at Bandar Abbas’s fish market, says business has slowed and that making ends meet has become increasingly difficult.
“Fishing boats can’t go out as freely as before the war, and our movement is restricted,” he says, adding that several of his colleagues in the city have been killed in attacks.
Anvar Sadat, who works at the fish market in Bandar Abbas
“This place was hell,” says Abdul Salam, a 45-year-old garbage collector. The beaches, particularly those near the port, were among the most dangerous places during the height of the war, he says, describing heavy attacks that forced him to stop working almost entirely to avoid the risk.
Life on the island, however, has been different, Farouq explains as he steers into the small, dimly lit port of Hormuz Island, his last crossing of the day before heading back to his family for the night.
Hassan, 28, cafe owner – has run a cafe on the island for eight years
Hormuz Island has long been known as a kind of “hippy paradise”, a place Iranians have come to regard as “free”. Artists and creatives moved here from bigger cities in search of peace; women swim in bathing suits, writers and painters find space to work, and life moves slower. There is “love and magic” here, as Yashar, a 35-year-old surfer, puts it, “a different rhythm”.
A group of local women swimming off the coast of Hormuz Island
Life here has changed little, Yashar says, although the war has brought some new restrictions, and a handful of attacks, mostly on infrastructure. The roughly 8,000 residents are trying to support each other, and to preserve the sense of freedom that has set the island apart, he adds.
The government has closed off parts of Hormuz Island’s north, but beyond the now restricted areas, life has continued, he explains. “As long as you don’t go north, they leave you alone,” he says of the army.
Omran, a 45-year-old tour guide – the tourism sector has been hit by the conflict
The Majara hotel, also known as Rainbow accommodation, is one of Hormuz’s attractions. It has been closed since the beginning of the war
“The tourism sector has taken the biggest hit,” says Omran, a 45-year-old tour guide, adding that he prefers to go by his first name only. “Guesthouses and homestays remain closed, as do restaurants and many cafes.” Visitors have largely stopped coming since the war, dealing a heavy blow to an island whose economy depends on tourism and fishing, both of which have been disrupted.
The Salt valley on Hormuz Island, one of the island’s tourist attractions
From the higher parts of the island, Omran says, it is possible to see deep into the strait on clear days, when the haze lifts and the humid air clears, all the way to the mountains of Khasab in Oman.
Residents have climbed up these barren mountains of red and white stone, at times watching the war unfold in the distance. Tankers remain stranded in the strait, explosions can be heard regularly. Yet residents also say the war has not driven them from the island.
Khaleh Kaniz, a 67-year-old painter who was born and raised on Hormuz, laughs when asked whether she had considered leaving in February, at the start of the war.
“Why should we leave? Where would we go? Our homes and our lives are here.”

items.title: Middle East Oil Flows Near Prewar Levels Defy Hormuz Attacks - gCaptain
items.summary: Middle East Oil Flows Near Prewar Levels Defy Hormuz Attacks  gCaptain
items.content:
The Soho Square, a crude oil tanker sailing under the flag of Liberia, is at anchor in the Galveston Bay as it makes it’s way to the Port of Houston shortly after U.S. President Donald Trump announced a 60-day waiver of the Jones Act shipping law, in Texas City, Texas, U.S. March 18, 2026. REUTERS/Antranik Tavitian
Middle East Oil Flows Near Prewar Levels Defy Hormuz Attacks
By Julian Lee (Bloomberg) — Oil shipments from the Middle East are showing little sign of buckling in the face of Iran’s more frequent and damaging attacks on merchant ships in the region.
Crude and condensate flows from the Persian Gulf hit a high of 24.6 million barrels a day in the week to Oct. 18, according to data provider Kpler. However, shipments are volatile and figures for the average of October to date remain below prewar levels. Loadings tend to happen in bunches, with ships traveling in convoys through the Strait of Hormuz , shuttling cargoes to tankers waiting outside the waterway before returning to reload.
Figures from rival data firm Vortexa don’t show the same weekly surge, highlighting the difficulty of establishing export levels as most tankers are currently operating with their positioning signals turned off. It pegs flows over the same seven-day period at 18 million barrels a day. Both companies estimate flows before the conflict was at least 18.5 million barrels a day.
The continued strong volumes despite the Iranian attacks show the desire for Middle Eastern producers to keep moving their barrels. Oil forms the backbone of the countries’ economies and they’ve been competing for customers in recent months to make up for billions of dollars of missed sales during the conflict.
For October so far, Kpler pegs Middle East flows at 16.7 million barrels a day, while Vortexa puts it at 15.4 million. Kpler aggregates its numbers from Hormuz transits, net flows via ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, exports through Red Sea ports and those on the Gulf of Oman in the United Arab Emirates and Oman. The Vortexa numbers sum shipments from Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Iran, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Oman.
The resilience comes as producers including Iraq are sending more volumes through Hormuz while Saudi Arabia is sending oil out from both its Persian Gulf and Red Sea coast. The kingdom boosted production by a third in September to over 8 million barrels a day, recovering from the lowest in more than three decades in the previous month. The UAE, one of the most successful in moving tankers through Hormuz, has pushed its production to record-high levels, according to the International Energy Agency.
These efforts appear to be holding up in spite of a spate of attacks in the waterway that’s also sunk at least one container ship this month. UK Maritime Trade Operations, a unit of the country’s navy, has reported 32 attacks on ships around the Arabian peninsula so far this month, compared with 16 in the whole of September. Some of these have struck ships’ engine rooms, inflicting more severe damage.
“Attacks on merchant vessels around the Strait have increased sharply in recent weeks,” Morgan Stanley analysts including Martijn Rats wrote in a note. Still, “oil flow through the strait has remained relatively resilient,” they added.
Shipments are proving strong with fleets owned by the producing countries and a few gutsy shipowners keeping crude flows close to last month’s levels that were the highest since the conflict began. The UAE, Saudi Arabia and Kuwait are among nations that have shuttled their oil through Hormuz in their own tankers, and delivered the cargo to customers’ vessels outside the strait.
The levels are also significant because of the complete loss of Iran’s exports following a US blockade of the country’s ports. Both Kpler and Vortexa estimate the Islamic Republic was shipping close to 2 million barrels a day in February.
The assessments of Mideast flows are subject to change as tankers operating in the Persian Gulf and Red Sea with their automatic information systems switched off make real-time tracking more complicated. The process is hampered further by the withholding of satellite imagery over the region. As a result, shipments are frequently only recorded several days after they occur, leading to upward revisions.
The shuttling service and the tendency for tankers to move in convoys have also made exports lumpy at times, with brief surges followed by periods of relative slowdown.
For example, satellite images of the biggest Saudi oil terminal in the Persian Gulf show five very large crude carriers loading at the seven moorings on Oct. 12 and 13, but the number had fallen to just one on Oct. 20. The pattern is similar at other oil ports in the Persian Gulf and on the Red Sea.

items.title: Gold ETFs to Watch Amid Fed Rate Hike & Oil Risks - Yahoo Finance Singapore
items.summary: Gold ETFs to Watch Amid Fed Rate Hike & Oil Risks  Yahoo Finance Singapore
items.content:
Gold prices have been under pressure this year. A stronger U.S. dollar and the Fed's hawkish stance continue to weigh on its prices.
Note that the Fed enacted the first rate hike of this year in September. There are expectations of another Fed rate hike this year. However, rising geopolitical tensions could support bullion by boosting safe-haven demand.
While the prospect of another U.S. interest-rate hike may limit near-term gains, expectations that the Fed could avoid further tightening in 2027 may help support gold prices over the longer term, per Bloomberg, as quoted on Yahoo Finance.
Rising oil prices, driven by renewed attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, have added to concerns about energy supply disruptions and persistent inflation. Higher energy costs could complicate the Federal Reserve's efforts to contain inflation.
New York Fed president John Williams indicated that another rate hike may be appropriate this year, while suggesting that additional tightening may not be necessary in 2027.
This outlook creates a mixed environment for bullion. Higher interest rates generally weigh on gold because the metal does not generate interest income, making interest-bearing assets more attractive. However, if investors begin anticipating an end to the tightening cycle, gold could regain support as the opportunity cost of holding the metal becomes less of a concern.
Oil Prices Contribute to Another Layer of Uncertainty
Developments in the Middle East could also influence gold's performance. Renewed attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz have heightened concerns about global energy supplies, supporting oil prices and increasing the risks of another inflationary shock.
Gold could benefit if escalating geopolitical tensions prompt investors to seek safe-haven assets. Sustained increases in energy prices could push inflation higher, potentially encouraging the Fed to maintain restrictive monetary policy for longer, whereas further disruptions to energy supplies could support investor interest in precious metals.
Gold ETFs may remain sensitive to policy expectations and developments in the Middle East. Rather than assuming that rising oil prices will automatically lift bullion due to increased safe-haven demand, investors should watch whether inflation risks translate into higher interest-rate expectations, which could weigh on the metal price.

Image caption, Witkoff (R) said there was still important work to do after the meeting with Putin (L)
By Steve Rosenberg Russia Editor ,Â  Reporting from Moscow
After two days of diplomacy â in Norway's capital and Russia's St Petersburg â is the war in Ukraine any closer to ending?
"Good and constructive" is how Norway's prime minister described Tuesday's talks between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, US President Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and European representatives.
In Oslo, the idea of a trilateral meeting at leaders' level was floated. The hope was that Steve Witkoff's trip to Russia would pave the way for President Vladimir Putin, Zelensky and Trump to meet and agree an end to the fighting.
But Putin has shown little desire to share a table with Zelensky - unless that table is in Moscow.
The Kremlin says it may be willing to resume trilateral talks next month in Abu Dhabi, but only at the technical level.
In a post on X, Steve Witkoff himself conceded that "there is still important work to do", though he claimed "President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end..."
Russia says it is ready to resume talks with Ukraine and US to end war
Trump and Zelensky at loggerheads despite new optimism
US citizen Stephen Hubbard freed by Russia as Trump envoy meets Putin
For me, the most telling statement of the day was from Vladimir Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov. He took part in the St Petersburg talks.
Ushakov said that Steve Witkoff had told President Putin about the discussions in Oslo and (as Witkoff viewed them) "new approaches from the Europeans and Kyiv".
The Kremlin adviser was clearly unimpressed by what he heard.
"In terms of resolving the Ukraine crisis, there wasn't much there that was useful," commented Ushakov.
Later Russian state TV asked him about the prospects for peace.
"I don't know how close we are getting," Yuri Ushakov said, "but things are moving in that direction."
It seems that President Putin doesn't feel under pressure right now to end the war.
He knows that Ukraine's air defences are under severe strain.
He knows that winter is coming and may well view the cold weather as an opportunity to pound Ukraine into submission.
He knows, too, that there is a US president in the White House who clearly wants a bigger, better, more profitable relationship with Moscow.
Image caption, Despite a "constructive" meeting between Witkoff and Zelensky in Oslo, Norway, the idea of a US-Russia-Ukraine trilateral summit does not seem to have taken hold
In recent days Donald Trump has paused some sanctions on Moscow, has agreed to buy Russian diesel and expressed biting criticism of President Zelensky.
That suits Russia just fine. It eases the pressure on the Kremlin leader.
"Right now Trump is the only leader in the Western world who is doing something for peace," Russian MP and TV anchor Evgeny Popov says.
"Doing something for peace, but a peace on your terms?" I respond. "Is that what you want?"
A Putin-Zelensky-Trump trilateral may not be imminent.
But in China next month a meeting between Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping may well take place on the fringes of the Apec summit.
Some commentators here are already dubbing it "The New Yalta" - a reference to the Yalta Conference of 1945, where Stalin, Churchill and Roosevelt met to plan the political and territorial reorganisation of post-war Europe.
"Russia, China and the United States are the only superpowers right now in the world," Evgeny Popov says. "Of course, it will be good for the entire world if our leaders meet in China."
After nearly five years of war, that would put Vladimir Putin exactly where he wants to be - at the top table of global politics.

Gold Declines Towards $4,120 as Iran Conflict and Federal Reserve Outlook Remain in Focus
Gold coin ©PIX1861 Gold prices declined on Wednesday as investors assessed uncertainty surrounding efforts to end the conflict between the United States and Iran, alongside expectations for US interest rates and the potential inflationary effects of higher energy costs.
At 02:36 ET (06:36 GMT), spot gold was down 0.2% at $4,117.31 per ounce, while US gold futures fell 0.2% to $4,134.92 per ounce.
Other precious metals also traded lower. Silver declined 1.2% to $57.2955 per ounce, platinum lost 1.8% to $1,627.45, and spot palladium decreased 1.6% to $1,088.40.
The US Dollar Index edged up 0.1% to 101.80, adding to the market conditions affecting dollar-denominated commodities.
Gold has fallen more than 1% since the beginning of the week and remains approximately 20% below its level when the US-Iran conflict began in late February.
The conflict has disrupted energy supplies and contributed to higher oil prices, complicating the inflation outlook and expectations for monetary policy.
Higher interest rates can affect demand for gold because the metal does not generate interest income, making interest-bearing assets comparatively more attractive.
Oil Price Movements Reflect Uncertainty Over Iran Negotiations
Oil prices stabilised on Wednesday after retreating from a five-month high during the previous session.
The decline followed reports suggesting that diplomatic efforts could lead to an agreement to end the conflict. However, a diplomat subsequently dismissed suggestions that a settlement was imminent.
Gold prices initially increased as oil declined following the reports of possible negotiations, before reversing those gains when energy prices recovered.
The US dollar and government bond yields also moved lower during the period of fluctuating oil prices.
Market participants continued to assess the potential implications of the conflict for global energy supplies, inflation and economic activity.
The relationship between energy prices and inflation expectations remains particularly relevant to gold, given the influence of monetary policy expectations on demand for non-interest-bearing assets.
US Treasury securities with longer maturities gained as oil prices retreated and economic data indicated softer conditions in parts of the US economy.
September housing starts declined, while pending home sales fell to a record low, providing further evidence of reduced activity in the housing market.
The figures added to the economic information being considered ahead of the Federal Reserve's next monetary policy meeting, scheduled for 27–28 October.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's comments on Friday did not materially change market expectations for the upcoming decision.
Investors continued to anticipate that the central bank would leave its benchmark interest rate unchanged at the October meeting.
Market pricing indicated a probability of less than 17% that the Fed would increase rates by 25 basis points at that meeting.
However, inflation remains above the central bank's 2% target, and traders were assigning approximately an 85% probability to another interest rate increase before the end of the year.
Warsh's remarks came ahead of the Federal Reserve's communications blackout period, which begins on Saturday and restricts public commentary from policymakers before the meeting.
With limited additional guidance expected from central bank officials, investors are monitoring economic indicators, Treasury yields and developments in the Middle East for information that could influence interest rate expectations.
Gold and other precious metals remained under pressure during Wednesday's trading as markets continued to evaluate the interaction between energy prices, inflation and the Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook.

items.content:
If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, Warren Buffett Says This Is the Smartest Move Investors Can Make
After a year of record-breaking gains, major market indexes are wobbling. The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) has fallen by nearly 2% over the last week, as of this writing, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC) is down by more than 4% in that time.
Much of the sell-off is stemming from the tech sector, with artificial intelligence (AI) spending under the microscope. Rising bond yields have driven up borrowing costs, making it more expensive for AI hyperscalers to continue building data centers and related infrastructure. If big tech companies pull back on AI spending, it could cause a ripple effect across the broader market.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
At this point, it's too soon to tell whether this volatility is a blip on the radar or the beginning of a deeper drawdown. Regardless of what's coming, though, Warren Buffett has one tried-and-tested strategy that can set your portfolio up for success.
Image source: Getty Images. An industry's potential has limits
In a 1999 essay for Fortune , Warren Buffett issued a warning to investors. The stock market was reaping the rewards of the dot-com boom, with the S&P 500 surging by nearly 200% over the previous four years, but Buffett predicted stock prices would fall.
He also emphasized that when an industry is poised to transform society, it's especially important to choose your investments carefully. Buffett mentioned airlines as an example, noting that while air travel itself has had a monumental impact on our lives, 129 airlines had filed for bankruptcy over the previous 20 years.
Buffett's 1999 warning eventually rang true, as the dot-com bubble officially popped in early 2000 -- leading to a bear market that would last more than two years. Hundreds of tech stocks crashed and burned, despite the internet's revolutionary impact on the world.
"The key to investing is not assessing how much an industry is going to affect society, or how much it will grow," Buffett said in the Fortune essay, "but rather determining the competitive advantage of any given company and, above all, the durability of that advantage."
When the dot-com bubble burst, overvalued stocks crashed the hardest. These companies earned explosive returns when the bubble was building, but many had unsustainable business models, poorly managed finances, or inexperienced leadership teams that couldn't navigate the bear market.
Now, we could be facing a similar situation. AI, as a technology, could transform the world. But not every company in the AI space will thrive. Many tech stocks have seen eye-popping returns this year, but it's likely that at least a few of them have been driven by hype and are overvalued right now.
This doesn't mean that all stocks will struggle over time, though. Since the start of the dot-com bear market in March 2000, for example, the S&P 500 has soared by more than 715%. While many companies failed, some tech stocks of the era -- like Apple , Amazon , and Microsoft -- went on to become industry-leading giants.
Overvalued stocks from weak companies will be hit the hardest whenever the next bear market arrives. Companies with strong fundamentals and a durable competitive advantage, however, have the best chance at recovering and going on to earn positive long-term returns.

items.title: The Stock Market is Flashing Several Warning Signs at Once. Does That Mean a Crash is Imminent? - The Motley Fool
items.summary: The Stock Market is Flashing Several Warning Signs at Once. Does That Mean a Crash is Imminent?  The Motley
items.content:
There have been many headlines recently about the stock market flashing warning signs. I've even written some of them . However, even when several signs flash at once, they don't mean a crash is imminent because they don't all tell us the same thing.
Instead, what they do signal is that now is the time to be more prepared. Here's how to read these signs and prepare your portfolio for what could lie ahead.
The stock market regularly experiences meaningful downdrafts. It has historically corrected (a 10% or more decline) roughly once every 18 months and tumbled into a bear market (a 20% or more drop) about once every six years. However, it doesn't move in that exact pattern. That's why investors are always looking for signs that another meaningful decline could be on the horizon.
One sign that has historically preceded a major decline is an elevated CAPE ratio (cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio). It measures whether the market is undervalued or overvalued relative to its historical inflation-adjusted earnings record. It's currently at 40.5; it's the second-highest reading in 150 years. Its prior peak was just before the dot-com crash. It was last above 40 in late 2021, right before the 2022 rate-driven bear market.
Speaking of rates, the Federal Reserve just started raising interest rates for the first time in three years. According to data from LPL Financial , the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC +0.58% ) has declined in five of the last six Fed rate-hike cycles (including 2022).
Finally, there's margin debt, which has surged 49% over the past year. According to data from Fundstrat Global Advisors, the market has declined five out of six times when margin debt has surged 45% or more year-over-year since 1960.
While all that sounds foreboding, none of these signs mean a crash is forthcoming, as they're not perfect predictors. For example, while a high CAPE ratio is a strong indicator of lower market returns over the longer term, it doesn't mean the market will crash next year. For example, it was above 30 in 2018. The next year, the S&P 500 rose 29%. It's also worth noting that the S&P 500 didn't decline during the 1997 rate-hike cycle (though that was only a 25-basis-point increase). Meanwhile, the S&P 500 was up 12 months following a 45% (or more) year-over-year increase in margin debt one out of every six times. For example, it last hit that level in October 2025, but was up 10.9% 12 months later.
So, we shouldn't read all these signs as imminent warnings of a crash. Instead, they should serve more as a reminder that the market does correct from time to time, and we need to ensure our portfolios remain prepared for the next downturn.
One way we can do that is by selling lower-conviction holdings to raise cash and by trimming positions where current valuations require perfect execution to deliver acceptable returns. That would build cash to capitalize on a meaningful decline in the coming months.
Now's also the time to build a watch list of stocks you want to buy if there is a downdraft. For example, Alphabet ( GOOG -1.63% ) ( GOOGL -1.65% ) is one of my higher-conviction holdings. It has a dominant search business and a growing cloud business, which is just scratching the surface of its AI potential. However, at 26 times forward earnings, Alphabet isn't cheap enough for me to add to right now, given that the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 index trades at about 21.5 times forward earnings. It's also investing heavily in AI ($180 billion to $190 billion this year), increasing its risks. While Alphabet's AI investments could drive meaningful growth in the coming years, I'd like a little more margin of safety. If Alphabet's stock got down closer to $300 per share (around 22.5x forward earnings), I'd start buying more.

With the market flashing lots of warning signs these days, it's easy to become fearful that it's about to crash. However, there's no guarantee this will happen, as these aren't perfect predictors. Meanwhile, even if a downdraft did happen, it's far better to see one not as a threat but as an opportunity. The best way to do that is to use the warning signs as a signal to be better prepared by building cash and a watch list now, so you can capitalize on any potential opportunities that may arise in the near term.

items.summary: Exclusive: Officials say Miatta Fahnbulleh minded not to give approval in victory for climate campaignersMiatta Fahnbulleh is minded to reject the giant Rosebank oilfield, sources have told the Guardian, in what would be a blow for the North Sea energy industry and a major victory for climate campaigners.After approving the smaller Jackdaw gasfield on Wednesday, offici
items.content:
Miatta Fahnbulleh with Douglas Alexander (left), the Scotland secretary, and John Healey, the chancellor, on a visit to a Shell gas terminal in Peterhead on Wednesday. Photograph: Paul Reid/PA
Miatta Fahnbulleh with Douglas Alexander (left), the Scotland secretary, and John Healey, the chancellor, on a visit to a Shell gas terminal in Peterhead on Wednesday. Photograph: Paul Reid/PA
Energy secretary leaning towards rejecting Rosebank oilfield
Exclusive: Officials say Miatta Fahnbulleh minded not to give approval in victory for climate campaigners
Miatta Fahnbulleh is minded to reject the giant Rosebank oilfield, sources have told the Guardian, in what would be a blow for the North Sea energy industry and a major victory for climate campaigners.
After approving the smaller Jackdaw gasfield on Wednesday, officials say the energy secretary is leaning towards refusing approval for what would be one of the biggest oilfields in the North Sea.
But she could still be overruled by Andy Burnham, who may hear different representations from the chancellor, John Healey. A final decision is expected before the end of this year.
In comments that will be read as a signal of her intent, Fahnbulleh told the Guardian that the rationale behind Jackdaw did not apply to Rosebank, saying the UK would rely on gas as it made the transition to net zero and that it would be better to take it from relatively low-carbon sources in the North Sea than importing it.
“One is a gasfield that caters for the domestic market, while the other is an oilfield that is mainly for export,” she said. “It is right that we judge each application in its own right, and it is absolutely critical that the decision is consistent with our climate obligations, our carbon budgets and the end destination we need to get to with the energy transition.”
In contrast, Healey told ITV he expected “oil and gas” revenues to contribute to a new energy wealth fund, a suggestion he is anticipating new oil revenues. Burnham would be expected to make the final call if there is conflict on the decision.
A map showing active oil and gas fields in UK waters Labour MPs warned on Wednesday there would be a major pushback in the party if Rosebank was approved, though most are prepared to accept the arguments that Jackdaw was a necessity as part of the transition to net zero.
MPs are understood to have discussed ways of forcing or encouraging a parliamentary vote on Rosebank should it be approved, as a way of expressing dissent.
Officials say Fahnbulleh has not yet taken a final decision on Rosebank. The field would emit about seven times the carbon of Jackdaw and Fahnbulleh is understood to believe that it would do less for UK energy security, given most of the oil would be exported.
A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “This is speculation. As the energy secretary has said, each project will be assessed on its own merits.”
On a visit to Aberdeen, Fahnbulleh said she had been satisfied that Jackdaw, which is due to begin producing gas within weeks and will add an estimated 36m tonnes of carbon emissions, would not violate the UK’s climate commitments.
“As we make the transition, we are going to need gas,” she said. “At a point when we have got conflict in the Middle East that is triggering an energy crisis, energy security is vital, and homegrown energy is key.”
She admitted, however, it would not help achieve the government’s main energy target of bringing down bills, saying: “This is not about bills.”
Fahnbulleh on a visit to St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeen on Wednesday. Photograph: Lauren Hurley/No 10 Downing Street The UN Environment Programme has recommended that global carbon emissions be cut by nearly a fifth in the next four years, and by close to half within a decade, to avoid overshooting climate targets by a disastrous margin.
The Jackdaw announcement could boost Labour’s position in north-east Scotland , where much of the industry is based and where unions have been campaigning heavily for the permits to be granted.
But it is likely to cause angst among some Labour MPs, especially those in seats where they face a challenge from the Green party.
One Labour MP close to the energy secretary said she knew her credibility was “on the line” and that she was able to show she was pragmatic by approving Jackdaw but drawing the line at Rosebank. “She’s putting up a fight and I want to be supportive of Miatta – I understand what she is fighting,” they said.
But they said the decision would ultimately come down to Burnham. “Andy is not a climate guy – he is under pressure. If he wants to do it, he’ll do it.”
Several serving ministers have said they would find Rosebank a more difficult decision to back and it would cause greater problems in their constituencies.
The former minister Catherine West said climate change “is not a future threat but a present reality” and that the answer to job losses in the North Sea was not to “double down on new fossil fuel developments”.
Afzal Khan, the Labour MP for Manchester Rusholme and chair of the all-party parliamentary group on climate change, said: “Approving projects on the scale of Rosebank, on top of today’s decision to approve Jackdaw, cannot be justified.”
Burnham is seeking more ways to lower energy bills, telling MPs on Wednesday that ministers would consider whether standing charges could be removed from gas bills to ease cost pressures on households.
While Labour’s 2024 election manifesto committed to a ban on new drilling licences in the North Sea, the companies behind Jackdaw and Rosebank oilfield project have sought approval for existing licences.
The Greens said on Wednesday they intended to fight seats directly on the issue of Jackdaw and Rosebank. The Green MP Carla Denyer said: “We have identified dozens of seats where we are Labour’s main challenger and the climate is one of the top issues and voters have been mobilised by the heatwave and wildfires.
“Our strong advice to Labour MPs is to stand up to Andy Burnham and his act of climate violence, both to save your seats and, far more importantly, to protect the planet for future generations.”
Fahnbulleh has promised that future revenues from the North Sea will be spent on green energy projects through a new energy wealth fund. She said the fund would be given £2bn in the budget.
“When we have tax revenues that are coming from the oil and gas industry, it is right that we invest that in the transition we need to make in energy,” she said, adding that the money would be spent on renewables, nuclear and other clean energy schemes.
However, she could not say exactly which tax revenues would be given to the new fund, or how much that might generate. “The chancellor will make those details clear in the budget,” she said.

items.title: Russia says Ukraine must make "necessary decisions" to end war as Witkoff meets Putin - CBS News
items.summary: Russia says Ukraine must make "necessary decisions" to end war as Witkoff meets Putin  CBS News
items.content:
Progress toward a negotiated resolution to Russia's war on Ukraine is "theoretically possible," Kremlin officials said Wednesday as U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg, but any headway will require Ukraine's leaders to make "necessary decisions," according to Russian state media.
If Ukraine fails to make those decisions, the situation for the country "will be worse," the officials said, according to Russian state news agency TASS.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted by Russian news agencies as saying Moscow would study proposals on the Ukraine war brought to St. Petersburg by Witkoff, but that the talks would take a long time.
During Witkoff's meeting with Putin, he and the Russian leader confirmed that Stephen Hubbard , a U.S. citizen jailed in Russia for more than four years, had been released from custody. President Trump said Putin agreed to free the American with "no 'swap' necessary," but he also said it wouldn't have happened had the U.S. not prevented new sanctions against Moscow from taking effect last week. Witkoff told Putin he was a "humanitarian" for releasing Hubbard, sparking backlash in the U.S.
State media said Russian officials told Witkoff on Wednesday that a meeting between Mr. Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping was "possible," referring to an idea the White House has also floated, but Ukrainian officials have balked at as it would sideline them from talks on their own country's fate.
Russian President Vladimir Putin shakes hands with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff at Constantine Palace in St. Petersburg, Russia, Oct. 21, 2026.
After Putin and Witkoff's meeting, a U.S. official told CBS News that the Russians and Ukrainians had agreed to the resumption of trilateral talks with the U.S. at the technical level.
According to a Kremlin transcript, Putin's senior foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov said that the Russian leader told Witkoff that Moscow was prepared, in principle, to resume the talks in early November. Ushakov also said the talks would involve building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the war.
But Ushakov also said that the proposals brought to St. Petersburg by Witkoff, which he attributed to Ukraine and the European Union, "contained little that was useful in the context of resolving the Ukrainian crisis."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Fox News on Wednesday that he believed trilateral talks between himself, Mr. Trump and Putin were the best way to resolve the conflict, and that he would not accept any resolution crafted by China, Russia and the U.S., saying: "Don't talk about us without us."
Zelenskyy also said any negotiated end to the war would need to be approved by Ukraine's Parliament.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio told journalists on a separate trip Wednesday that Witkoff held "positive" talks with Zelenskyy on Tuesday in Oslo before traveling to Russia, and that he would share ideas discussed with Zelenskyy with the Russian side in an attempt to "make some progress."
After that meeting with Witkoff in Oslo, Zelenskyy thanked Washington for restoring U.S. intelligence sharing on Russian strikes, after saying this week that his country had stopped receiving advance warnings of imminent Russian missile strikes.
"We are thankful that intelligence works," Zelenskyy told reporters in Oslo. He said the early warnings for ballistic missiles were "very, very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians."
Zelenskyy told Fox on Wednesday, however, that access to data from the Starshield satellite network, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink system, remained "limited" in Ukraine , but that Rubio was working on it and expected full access to be restored.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, right, and Masud Gharahkhani, the president of Norway's Parliament, speak to journalists on Oct. 21, 2026, in Oslo.
Witkoff planned to return to Oslo for more consultations with European officials following his visit to Russia, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said.
"I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy," Støre told Norwegian broadcaster NRK on Wednesday morning.
Zelenskyy was still in Oslo on Wednesday, where he said "a lot depends on whether the American side manages to hear something new from Russia today."
The diplomacy comes after weeks of friction between Kyiv and Washington, with Mr. Trump criticizing Zelenskyy for Ukraine's continued response to relentless, deadly Russian strikes on energy and civilian infrastructure with Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil infrastructure.
Mr. Trump announced an " energy ceasefire " earlier in the month, claiming both sides had agreed to halt strikes on each other's energy infrastructure, but within hours Russia launched new missile attacks on Ukrainian refineries and other sites, and neither Ukraine nor Russia ever confirmed agreeing to a truce of any kind.
The U.S. president also announced a deal with Moscow on Oct. 10 for Russia to release millions of tons of diesel fuel over the next several months, which Zelenskyy labeled a sign of "weakness."
Russian state media said the first shipment of diesel had been dispatched for the U.S. on Wednesday.

items.title: Zelenskyy says early warning system for Russian missile attacks resumes
items.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the change happened after talks with his American counterparts, including a phone call with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
items.content:
Zelenskyy says early warning system for Russian missile attacks resumes Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the change happened after talks with his American counterparts, including a phone call with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Zelenskyy says early warning system for Russian missile attacks resumes
Rescuers with a search dog look for victims among the rubble of a house after a Russian air attack in Kharkiv, Ukraine, Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026.
KYIV, Ukraine — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday that Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners about incoming Russian missiles following recent strikes that he said occurred without enough notice, leaving civilians vulnerable.
A conversation with President Volodmyr Zelenskyy of Ukraine
For at least a week, the Ukrainian leader has said that his country has not received early warnings about ballistic missiles aimed at the capital. Such intelligence, he said, saves lives by allowing the public to be alerted and giving military units time to try to intercept the missiles.
Zelenskyy said the change happened after talks with his American counterparts, including a phone call with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
"We are thankful that intelligence works now, and I'm speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming," Zelenskyy said on a visit to Norway. "So we are thankful to American side now that it works."
Speaking to reporters in India, Rubio acknowledged mutual frustration between the U.S. and Ukraine over intelligence sharing and weapons supplies but emphatically denied that the Trump administration has made any changes to previous policy on either issue.
In other developments, Russia unleashed another missile and drone blitz of civilian areas in Ukraine, killing at least nine people, officials said, as Zelenskyy sought more American and European help.
Zelenskyy was joined in Norway by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, who has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement to end the war. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb also met with the Ukrainian president in Norway's capital.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyj, Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, and Finnish President Alexander Stubb speak during a press conference on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026 in Oslo, Norway.
Gahr Støre said Witkoff planned to fly to St. Petersburg on Wednesday to meet with Russian leaders, exchange ideas from the Oslo meeting and share proposals from European and American colleagues.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Moscow is willing to listen to new U.S. proposals about Ukraine but doesn't expect any "miracle" from Washington.
Trump makes Russia-friendly moves as he looks for a way to end the war with Ukraine
At the White House, President Donald Trump stepped up the pressure on Zelenskyy to come to an agreement with Russia as relations between the two men have soured again.
"We want Zelenskyy to make a deal," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. "We've given a lot to Ukraine. We've gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss."
If that doesn't happen, "I think it's going to be a very bad thing."
The conversation with Rubio came after Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers Monday that he believes "some political decision has been made to slow down ... support for us."
Ukraine has nearly run out of American-made Patriot air-defense interceptors that it needs to stop Russian ballistic missiles, according to Zelenskyy, who has pleaded for Washington to send more. But he said the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that other countries have purchased for Ukraine.
The Ukrainian leader also said speed restrictions were still in place on his country's use of Starshield, the military-grade version of U.S. company SpaceX's satellite internet service Starlink, hampering battlefield operations.
Trump also has waived sanctions on Russia, a move that Zelenskyy slammed as helping Putin push on with Moscow's full-scale invasion, which will hit the five-year mark in February.
Ukraine and the U.S. are at odds over Starshield. Here's what to know
Zelenskyy said he had "a substantive conversation" with Rubio.
"I am grateful for his readiness to help and his clear position," Zelenskyy said on social media.
Rubio, who arrived Tuesday in India on an official trip, denied that the U.S. is withholding assistance from Ukraine.
The Patriot ammunition Ukraine needs is in short supply and is also required elsewhere in the world, Rubio said.
"There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine," he said.
European countries, worried about Russia's plans on the continent and viewing Ukraine as a bulwark against Moscow's ambitions, are trying to take up the slack of any falloff in U.S. supplies, but some key assets are American-made.
European countries and European Union institutions have allocated 237 billion euros ($266 billion) to support Ukraine, compared with 115 billion euros ($129 billion) from the U.S., according to Germany's Kiel Institute, which tracks assistance to Kyiv.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas on Tuesday questioned whether U.S. negotiators have been honest brokers in peace efforts. Ukrainian officials say the Trump administration has encouraged Kyiv to surrender land to Russia in return for peace.
"Although American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for … one and a half years now," Ukraine has not surrendered on Putin's terms "because Europe has been supporting Ukraine," Kallas said.
Russian attacks cause power outages in 12 Ukrainian regions
Four people were killed and 27 others wounded, including children, in Russian missile and drone attacks on the Kyiv region over the past day, regional police said.
Three were killed and six were wounded in the Obukhiv district, where warehouses were damaged, police said. In the Bucha district, one woman was killed and 21 people were wounded, eight of them children, while hundreds of buildings were damaged, according to police.
On Tuesday morning, three people were killed and four injured when two vehicles caught fire in a Russian attack on the Kyiv-Odesa highway, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said. The dead included the driver of a shuttle bus that was hit. The bus transports people from Kyiv to the National Military Memorial Cemetery.
Two more people were killed in a Russian attack Tuesday on warehouses on the outskirts of Dnipro in central Ukraine, authorities said.
National grid operator Ukrenergo reported power outages in 12 regions of Ukraine following the Russian attacks.
The Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement that its forces carried out drone strikes on logistics centers, port infrastructure and three cargo ships in the port of Reni in the Odesa region. It said that another bulk carrier was hit at sea on its way to Odesa.
Meanwhile, air defenses intercepted 136 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions overnight, the ministry said.

items.title: Iran determined to keep uranium amid increased war odds, flurry of meetings
items.summary: Tehran had 'nothing new' to tell Washington after latest nuclear proposals reportedly offered by mediators.
items.content:
Share Iran determined to keep uranium amid increased war odds, flurry of meetings on social media
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, right, gestures to Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov during their meeting in Tehran, Iran, October 19, 2026 [Vahid Salemi/AP]
Tehran, Iran – There has been a flurry of diplomatic activity in the Middle East in recent days, with hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough to end the United States and Israel war on Iran.
Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir was in Tehran on Wednesday to discuss the war and recent tensions in Yemen. It comes against the backdrop of fears of a new breakout in conflict in the region.

list 2 of 3 UK approves development of Jackdaw gasfield in North Sea
list 3 of 3 Putin ready to resume three-way Ukraine peace talks
Despite this, Tehran has held firm to its position that the war will not end, and the Strait of Hormuz will not reopen, until the US accepts its conditions.
Iran maintains an unyielding stance on its contentious nuclear programme, which was a factor in the Trump administration’s decision to launch the war on February 28.
“Not a single gram of enriched uranium will be removed from Iran,” Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said late Tuesday after meeting Munir.
But he did not rule out downblending the highly enriched uranium inside the country under supervision from monitors, something Iran has offered before.
Iran’s authorities present the decades-old nuclear programme as a sovereign right and an achievement gained despite strikes, sabotage and assassinations. Rezaei described it as “national wealth” on Tuesday.
Iran has also used low-enriched uranium for civilian purposes like manufacturing radiopharmaceuticals and for power generation at the Bushehr plant in cooperation with Russia.
The authorities argue that surrendering the nuclear programme under military pressure would amount to capitulation, if it did not guarantee that Iran would not be left exposed to more attacks.
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly emphasised since the start of the war that he wanted to dismantle the Iranian nuclear programme. US Vice President JD Vance, however, suggested earlier this month that a “meaningful” reduction in the level of enrichment capacity may satisfy US demands.
Before Israeli and US attacks on Iran’s nuclear facilities in June 2025, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) estimated that Tehran possessed 440 kilogrammes (970 pounds) of uranium enriched up to 60 percent. A nuclear bomb would need enrichment of more than 90 percent.
The attacks, followed by further US-Israeli strikes on nuclear sites in 2026, severely damaged Iran’s nuclear infrastructure. With the IAEA unable to inspect key facilities, the current size, condition and whereabouts of much of Iran’s enriched uranium stockpile remain unverified.
Tehran has refused access to the IAEA to inspect its nuclear facilities since the war started, accusing the agency of advancing Western interests through adopting resolutions and referring the nuclear file to the United Nations Security Council .
Iranian authorities maintain they are not pursuing a bomb. But senior Iranian officials, like Rezaei, have publicly questioned the validity of being a party to the international nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty if Iran’s nuclear facilities and other infrastructure continue to be attacked.
Still, Iranian officials have hosted numerous foreign diplomats this week. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov was in Tehran on Monday after attending a meeting with Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries a day earlier. There were also indications of visits to Tehran by other Arab officials.
US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth is also reported to have met Israeli security officials earlier this week. These meetings did not appear to have decreased the prospects of renewed war.
But speaking at a conference for Iranian exporters in Tehran on Wednesday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi cautioned that the country faces threats of more attacks and expansive economic sanctions .
“The reality is that the country is truly in war conditions and the war continues. We have not reached peace conditions and are away from it, so all decisions must be made within war conditions,” he said.
Parliament speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf told Munir that Iran had “nothing new” to tell Washington and expected realisation of conditions offered in New York last month to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days.
Mediators did not publicly divulge details of their proposals to Tehran this week, but were told the US needed to build trust by accepting Iran’s conditions. These include returning to the June memorandum of understanding and recognising an Iran-Oman deal over temporary transit in the Strait of Hormuz .
US Navy sailors tend to a fighter jet on the flight deck of the USS George Washington in the Arabian Sea, September 11, 2026 [Ed Ou/Reuters] In addition to a pledge for immediate talks on a bigger deal regarding Iran’s nuclear issue, the memorandum included removing the US naval blockade on southern Iranian ports, waivers for oil sanctions, unfreezing Iranian assets and halting military action in Lebanon and other regional hotspots.
Ellie Geranmayeh, a senior policy fellow and deputy head of the Middle East and North Africa programme at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said it was clear that Tehran would be unwilling to give up its enriched uranium without guarantees of sanctions relief.
“The Iranians have made it very clear, and I see no evidence that’s changing, that they are willing to negotiate over the fate of the highly enriched uranium or access for international monitors, but that has to be directly linked with a very clear implementation protocol for US sanctions relief,” she told Al Jazeera. “We are very far from those types of negotiations at this stage.”
US media cited unnamed officials as saying on Tuesday that the Pentagon was sending the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and a Marine unit to the Middle East. That would present President Trump with a range of strike options after the US midterm elections on November 3.
Over recent weeks, Trump and his officials have further discussed a range of military operations, including hitting Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain to diminish nuclear facilities inside, and dropping the “mother of all bombs” on nuclear and energy facilities. They have also previously raised the idea of seizing Iran’s southern islands on the Strait of Hormuz and assassinating more Iranian officials.
Iran’s state-run Press TV cited an unnamed security official as saying on Wednesday that decision-makers in Tehran have chosen to advance “without any limitations or restraint” if there are more US and Israeli attacks or assassinations.

items.content:
US Stock Futures Edge Higher as SpaceX and Tesla Explore Merger and Meta Earnings Approach: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq, Wall Street
Wall Street NYSE stock exchange ©Shutterstock US stock futures traded mostly higher on Wednesday as investors assessed corporate earnings, developments in artificial intelligence investment and geopolitical uncertainty surrounding the conflict in the Middle East. Attention also turned to comments from Elon Musk about a potential merger between SpaceX and Tesla, reports concerning Anthropic's financial performance and Meta Platforms' forthcoming quarterly results.
US futures rise as investors assess earnings and oil prices
At 03:01 ET (07:01 GMT), S&P 500 futures were up 13 points, or 0.2%, while Nasdaq 100 futures gained 148 points, or 0.5%. Dow Jones futures were broadly unchanged.
Wall Street ended Tuesday's session with mixed results. The S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced, while the Nasdaq Composite closed slightly lower.
Oil prices fluctuated during the session following unconfirmed reports that Qatar and Pakistan had proposed renewed negotiations aimed at ending the conflict involving Iran. Brent crude briefly declined from approximately $112 to $106 per barrel before recovering.
The initial decline in energy prices coincided with gains in equities, which have recently been affected by concerns over borrowing costs and the scale of debt-financed investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure.
"The relief from energy that played out late in the European session meant equities rallied as investors overcame some of their earlier AI jitters," Deutsche Bank analysts said in a research note.
Brent subsequently returned to approximately $110 per barrel after reports of comments attributed to Iran's president concerning the possibility of further US military action.
Technology shares underperformed parts of the broader market. An index tracking semiconductor companies declined 0.29%, although it recovered much of its earlier losses. AI cloud infrastructure provider CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) also rebounded during the session.
SpaceX and Tesla establish committees to examine possible merger
SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) and Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) have formed committees to evaluate a potential combination of the two businesses, according to Elon Musk, who serves as chief executive of both companies.
Speaking to investors following SpaceX's quarterly earnings announcement, Musk said the committees had not reached an agreement on "the terms of any transaction."
Musk, who is not a member of either committee, said there was "no guarantee" that a merger would take place, although he considered there to be "a lot of merit" in combining the businesses.
Shares in both companies advanced in after-hours trading following the comments.
A potential transaction would bring together SpaceX's rocket launch and satellite operations with Tesla's electric vehicle and related technology businesses. No transaction terms or timetable have been announced.
SpaceX reported third-quarter revenue of $14.6 billion, an increase of more than 160% compared with the previous year and above analysts' expectations.
The company recorded profit of $4.4 billion, while capital expenditure reached $19.6 billion during the period.
The results marked SpaceX's second quarterly earnings publication since its initial public offering earlier in 2026.
Tesla is scheduled to report its quarterly financial results after Wednesday's market close.
Anthropic reports revenue growth alongside financial and operational risks
Artificial intelligence developer Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANTP) reported substantial revenue growth during the first half of the year, according to media reports citing disclosures associated with its potential initial public offering.
The company, which develops the Claude AI models, generated revenue of $16.3 billion during the six-month period.
Approximately 20% of that revenue came from two customers, highlighting the concentration of sales among a relatively small number of clients.
Anthropic indicated that a significant proportion of its revenue is expected to remain dependent on a limited customer base for the foreseeable future.
The company also identified uncertainty surrounding access to the computing infrastructure required to develop and operate its AI models.
Anthropic recorded a net loss exceeding $80 billion, compared with a loss of $13 billion in the corresponding period last year. The reported increase was largely attributed to an accounting adjustment.
Additional risks identified in the disclosures included potential legal liabilities arising from the use of artificial intelligence, including cybersecurity-related incidents.
Reports suggested that a future stock market listing could value Anthropic at approximately $2 trillion, although no confirmed IPO valuation was provided.
Meta earnings to provide update on AI investment plans
Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) is scheduled to release its quarterly earnings after Wednesday's closing bell, with investors focusing on revenue performance and the company's spending plans for artificial intelligence.
The owner of Facebook and Instagram has recently expanded its AI product portfolio following the September introduction of its Muse model.
According to the reported information, the product attracted millions of downloads following its launch, with applications including travel booking assistance and tools for small businesses.
Meta subsequently introduced an open-weight version of its Muse Spark model for coding applications.
The earnings announcement will provide an update on Meta's investment requirements as it expands its AI infrastructure and related services.
Large technology companies have committed substantial capital to advanced semiconductor purchases, computing capacity and data centre construction as they develop AI products.
Investors have increasingly focused on the relationship between these expenditures, financing requirements and the revenue generated by AI-related services.
Meta's results will therefore be examined for information on capital expenditure expectations and the financial contribution of its AI initiatives.
Nvidia reportedly considers additional investment in Firmus Grid
Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) is in discussions about investing hundreds of millions of dollars in Australian AI cloud infrastructure company Firmus Grid, according to a report by The Information.
Nvidia already holds an investment stake in Firmus and has invested in several other companies operating in the AI cloud infrastructure sector.
The reported discussions follow Firmus Grid's decision to abandon plans for an initial public offering in Australia earlier this month.
The company cited recent financial market volatility as a reason for withdrawing the proposed listing, which it said would not have been in shareholders' interests under the prevailing conditions.
Firmus had previously outlined plans for an IPO at a valuation exceeding $30 billion, potentially making it one of Australia's largest stock market listings.
The size, structure and timing of any additional Nvidia investment have not been confirmed.
US equity markets entered Wednesday's session with attention divided between corporate earnings, AI infrastructure financing and developments in the Middle East. The forthcoming results from Meta and Tesla, together with reported activity involving SpaceX, Anthropic and Nvidia, are among the company-specific developments being assessed by investors.

Wall Street Futures Rise as Corporate Earnings Support Technology Stocks: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq
Nasdaq sign on a tall building ©Dries Buytaert US stock index futures pointed to a higher opening on Wednesday, suggesting Wall Street could extend its gains from recent sessions as investors assessed quarterly earnings reports and prepared for further results from major technology companies.
Technology stocks were expected to contribute to the early advance, although individual companies recorded contrasting pre-market movements following their latest financial announcements.
SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) shares rose 8.8% in pre-market trading after the rocket and space technology company led by Elon Musk reported third-quarter earnings above market expectations, supported by a substantial increase in revenue.
Musk also confirmed that SpaceX and Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) had established independent special committees to examine a potential merger. No final decision regarding a transaction was announced.
Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI) advanced 12.2% before the opening bell after the data centre server manufacturer raised its revenue outlook for the first quarter of its fiscal year.
In contrast, Netflix (NASDAQ:NFLX) declined 6.8% in pre-market trading. The streaming company reported third-quarter earnings that exceeded analysts' estimates but issued revenue guidance below market expectations.
AT&T (NYSE:T) shares also fell, losing 5% despite the telecommunications company reporting third-quarter revenue and earnings above forecasts.
Investors were also awaiting quarterly results from Tesla, Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) and IBM (NYSE:IBM), all scheduled for release after Wednesday's market close.
The anticipated higher opening followed a mixed performance on Wall Street on Tuesday, when stocks recovered from an initial decline before giving back part of their gains later in the session.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 529.85 points, or 1%, to close at 52,495.88, its highest closing level in more than a month. The S&P 500 gained 21.84 points, or 0.3%, to 7,712.57, while the Nasdaq Composite slipped 6.07 points, or less than 0.1%, to 26,424.82.
Industrial conglomerate 3M (NYSE:MMM) contributed to the Dow's advance, with its shares rising 6% after the company reported third-quarter earnings above expectations and increased its full-year profit forecast.
Other Dow constituents, including Amgen (NASDAQ:AMGN), Merck (NYSE:MRK) and UnitedHealth (NYSE:UNH), also recorded gains.
Movements in energy prices influenced trading sentiment during Tuesday's session. US crude oil futures fell substantially after earlier increases, following a report suggesting that diplomatic efforts could lead to a reduction in tensions between the United States and Iran.
According to Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, negotiators from Qatar and Pakistan had presented a compromise proposal aimed at ending the conflict. The report cited a source suggesting that an announcement concerning a possible halt to the escalation could come during the week.
Neither the United States nor Iran had confirmed the reported proposal.
The decline in crude oil prices coincided with increased buying interest in equities, although investors remained attentive to geopolitical developments and forthcoming corporate earnings.
Among individual sectors, pharmaceutical stocks advanced, lifting the NYSE Arca Pharmaceutical Index by 2.8% to its highest closing level in two months.
Housing-related shares also gained, with the Philadelphia Housing Sector Index rising 2.6%.
Biotechnology, healthcare and airline stocks recorded increases alongside most other major market sectors.
Wednesday's session is expected to remain focused on corporate earnings, particularly the forthcoming announcements from Tesla, Meta Platforms and IBM, while developments in energy markets and US-Iran relations could also influence investor sentiment.

A 2027 turning point? Goldman, Citi see stabilising signs in China’s housing market
Encouraging holiday sales and shrinking supply point to recovery for country’s property sector, according to Goldman Sachs and Citi
As China’s housing market downturn enters its fifth year, global investment banks including Goldman Sachs and Citi say they expect the sector to pivot as soon as 2027, with expectations fuelled by signs of shrinking supply and robust sales over the National Day holiday in early October.
Citi holds a positive view on the sector and saw 2027 as a pivotal year for home price recovery in Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen. Home prices in China hit their lowest point in June 2024, according to Citi.
Shanghai became the first city to post positive year-on-year growth in secondary home prices in September, with prices rising 0.8 per cent, according to the National Bureau of Statistics on Monday.
“While we need further confirmation before declaring a sustained recovery, the evidence increasingly points to stabilising and potentially rising home prices in top cities, with most tier-two cities likely to lag,” said Griffin Chan, an analyst at Citi Research, in a report on Tuesday.

items.title: ​Europe stands by Ukraine – but how long can that last? - The Guardian
items.summary:

European Council President Antonio Costa, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels on October 16, 2026. Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty Images
European Council President Antonio Costa, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels on October 16, 2026. Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty Images
​Europe stands by Ukraine – but how long can that last?
As US support ebbs away, looming European elections and growing financial strains across the continent could fracture the precious coalition that has kept Ukraine afloat
E urope woke up last Friday to another belligerent outburst from Donald Trump – this time berating Ukraine’s wartime leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy again. Just a few days after his diesel deal with the Kremlin, the US president said Zelenskyy was more difficult to deal with than Vladimir Putin and blamed Ukraine’s leader for rocketing oil prices – without any reference to the impact of his own war on Iran.
The contrast in Europe was obvious. When Zelenskyy walked into the multi-coloured summit room of the European Council headquarters in Brussels that Friday morning, the EU’s 27 leaders burst into applause, getting to their feet to offer big hugs and brisk handshakes. European Council president António Costa told Zelenskyy and the media: “This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine ,” calling instead for increased pressure on Russia. Zelenskyy was thankful, pointedly saying he was happy to have “huge support” from “real leaders”.
The symbolism was powerful. As US support crumbles, Europe seems to be stepping up. According to the Kiel Institut’s Ukraine Support Tracker , Europe – including non-EU countries such as the UK and Norway – has spent €236bn supporting Ukraine from 2022 to April 2026, compared with a US outlay of €115bn.
While Trump is weakening sanctions, Europe is promising more. The EU has passed 21 rounds of sanctions against Russia and last year agreed to raise a €90bn loan for Ukraine – an unprecedented sum for a non-member state. Meanwhile the EU has opened accession negotiations with Kyiv and given shelter to 4.4million Ukrainian refugees.
Behind the declarations of Europe’s enduring support, the outlook is more complex and less encouraging for Ukraine, as it approaches its fifth winter since the launch of Russia’s all-out invasion.
First, Europe is not able to replace US military dominance in areas such as intelligence. This was brutally exposed by the disruption to the US SpaceX technologies that Ukraine uses in frontline drone operations and air-defences protecting civilians from Russian air attacks. Zelenskyy said the US had intentionally throttled its Starlink satellite internet access, a charge that senior figures in the Trump administration have denied.
Ukraine also depends on US-made Patriot interceptors capable of shooting down Russian ballistic missiles. Deepening the spat, Zelenskyy this week accused the Trump administration of preventing European countries from passing on their Patriot stocks to Ukraine.
Secondly, Europe’s monetary support for Ukraine is not evenly spread. Germany is the second-largest donor, having spent €54bn since the start of the war, a particularly crucial contribution since Trump ceased virtually all new US funding. But a report from the Kiel Institut describes this funding as “sizeable but not exceptional” given the scale of the German economy. Four Nordic countries together have given more than Germany, even though they total only a third of Germany’s population, the researchers note. The EU’s other big economies, France and Italy, give less than Germany.
The Nordic, Baltic and other north European states are Ukraine’s most generous donors when contributions are measured against national income, according to the Kiel Institut. Denmark, for instance, spends an equivalent to 4.17% of its gross domestic product supporting Ukraine, and Estonia 3.77%, compared with 1.49% spent by Germany, 1.1% by France, 1% by Italy and 0.86% by the UK. With Ukraine’s huge bill to defend itself growing, and Russia’s relentless attacks continuing to wreak a heavy toll, these more generous donors might arguably feel Europe’s biggest economies – and other western allies – could do more to shoulder these ever-rising costs.
Financial aid from 24 January 2022 to 31 August 2026 as a % of a country’s 2021 GDP. Illustration: Guardian graphic/Source: Kiel Institute for the World Economy Thirdly, and most critically, Europe’s support for Ukraine could be reaching its limits, as Europe enters a supercycle of elections in which the far-right are expected to make gains. National votes are due in Spain, France, Poland and Italy, four of the five biggest EU member states by population. Mujtaba Rahman , managing director for Europe at the Eurasia Group, argued that the biggest risk for Ukraine is not Trump’s opinions, but the potential for European support to fragment. There is a risk 2027 will be the year “when political reality, electoral reality, policy reality, economic reality catches up with Europe and prevents it being able to go further in its support for Ukraine”, he said.
France’s elections could be the most consequential. The far-right leader and frontrunner Marine Le Pen is seeking to present herself as the candidate to restore order and security, after days of rioting and looting across French cities. She has also vowed to cease aid to Ukraine within six months of taking office “because we simply cannot do it any more”. Speaking to the Financial Times (£) , Le Pen vowed to slash France’s contributions to the EU budget, which raises questions about a proposed €100bn fund for Ukraine in the upcoming 2028-34 budget cycle. Beyond Ukraine, her election could plunge the EU into a deep internal crisis that will consume political energies and attention.
US patience is running out with Ukraine as US special envoy Steve Witkoff meets with Vladimir Putin in Russia. Photograph: Kristina Solovyova/Reuters “European support for Ukraine is already fragmenting,” argued Rahman, who points out the €90bn loan for Ukraine was agreed by only 24 EU countries (Hungary, Czechia and Slovakia opted out). But a Le Pen victory could tilt the balance, especially if anti-Ukraine parties make gains in Spain, Poland and Italy. “Le Pen is the biggest gamechanger because she will provide cover for many other countries to say: ‘enough is enough, we can’t keep funding,’” Rahman said.
That scenario paints “a really dark picture for Ukraine, a really sad picture for Ukraine” he said. “Because it’s not about Ukraine’s performance on the battlefield – Ukraine has done a remarkable job of holding the line. This is the risk Europe has been talking about for a very long time, and has promised Ukraine many times it would not allow to happen: that through strategic patience, Russia gains in the negotiating room what it has not been able to gain on the battlefield. And that is precisely the risk Ukraine is now confronting.”
To head off this risk, EU leaders will seek to shore up support for Ukraine by agreeing another funding plan. The head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, confirmed that Kyiv has a €70bn funding gap in 2027, although she expects Ukraine’s other international partners to help raise the sum.
Jana Kobzová, co-director of the European Security Programme at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said an EU leaders summit in December will be the moment when “we should have a clear idea and mechanism” on providing the €70bn for Ukraine ahead of key elections. “I think the urgency and the consciousness on the side of the European leaders is already there.”
To some extent, EU Russia policy is protected, after a recent decision to keep sanctions in place for three years, avoiding the need for divisive rollover decisions every six months.
But a Le Pen victory in six months’ time could lead to a bigger problem than financing Ukraine, suggests Kobzová. “If there is a huge shift in Europe as a result of these elections that are going to affect the way the EU itself works, then Ukraine might become collateral damage.”

The framing stands in sharp contrast to the many rightwing and far-right voices who have sought to exploit the violence in France and Italy, linking it without evidence to migration while brushing over protesters’ wider demands.
