items.title: Meta fined $25bn for 'lies' over user data privacy
items.summary: The fine is the largest to date against Facebook's owner, larger than an $18bn deal with California.
items.content:
Image caption, Meta has been hit with numerous legal fines this year
Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp has been hit with the largest ever fine against it for its business practices.
A judge in New Mexico on Wednesday ordered the company to pay $25bn (Â£18.6bn) following a two-week trial earlier this year that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.
"The lies extend beyond Facebook's data practices as well," the judge said, adding they went to "the heart of Facebook's core business practices".
Meta's head lawyer CJ Mahoney said the ruling made it "all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico". The company intends to appeal, a move Mahoney said will be successful.
The fine is the largest to date against Meta, which has either been fined or agreed to settle several other lawsuits this year, including an $18bn deal with California over child safety.
New Mexico's lawsuit stemmed from the role of Meta, then still doing business as Facebook, in what became known as the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
That firm utilized data and information from millions of Facebook users as part of its work in political consulting, including on work related to the 2016 US Presidential election, which saw Donald Trump elected for the first time.
New Mexico had also accused Meta of intentionally misleading the public on how it benefitted from content that included hate speech, and how such rules against it were enforced. The jury found the company had intentionally misled the public on those claims, too.
Meta disputed those accusations. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online," Mahoney added.
Lawyers for New Mexico sued the company over many statements Meta executives had made over the years that user data was never shared with or accessed by third parties without a user's permission, when in reality it had been.
They claimed that the entire population of the state, roughly two million people, was impacted by Meta's dishonesty regarding the way it controlled user data. A jury found that Meta had violated state laws more than 40 million times.
"For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," New Mexico Attorney General RaÃºl Torrez said Wednesday.
"Today's result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable."
The state lawyers sought up to $40bn in fines against Meta. Meta had argued anything beyond $3.4bn would be unconstitutional.
Judge Francis Mathew on Wednesday was direct in his decision to fine Meta an amount roughly equal to its profits each quarter.
He said Meta's violations of law and misrepresentations to the public about how their Facebook data was used and shared were "willful" and spanned "more than 11 years", stretching from 2010 to 2021.
Communications between senior executives, including Mark Zuckerberg, were "designed to mislead the public", Judge Mathew wrote in his order.
While the full amount of the penalty against Meta, based on thousands of violations of state law, was calculated as $219bn, Judge Mathew reduced the penalty to the $25bn fine.
It follows a $5bn fine levied by the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 against the company over its data privacy practices.
New Mexico has been one of Meta's most notable adversaries in court. The state this year also fined Meta almost $1bn for misleading the public about the safety of its social media platforms for children.
The judge overseeing that lawsuit ultimately compared Meta to an industrial polluter of the air, with its form of pollution being "the psychological harm and sexual exploitation of children".
California and several other states had collectively sued Meta over similar issues related to a lack of child safety features on Meta's platforms and resulting harms to children.
Meta and the states reached a mutual settlement deal, which did not include a fine or any admission of wrongdoing, to end that case only a few days into what was expected to be a multi-week trial.

items.title: Jackdaw approval is a step towards a grownup North Sea policy
items.summary: Government decision is about how much oil and gas is sensible for UK to produce on the way to net zeroBusiness live – latest updatesAndy Burnham hit the nail on the (well)head in his first fortnight as prime minister when <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/jul/31/andy-burnham-risks-labour-revolt-nort
items.content:
The Jackdaw debate was always about tax receipts, jobs, the national balance of payments, relative emissions and the security from having domestic gas piped straight into the national network. Photograph: Adura/Reuters
The Jackdaw debate was always about tax receipts, jobs, the national balance of payments, relative emissions and the security from having domestic gas piped straight into the national network. Photograph: Adura/Reuters
Jackdaw approval is a step towards a grownup North Sea policy
Government decision is about how much oil and gas is sensible for UK to produce on the way to net zero
A ndy Burnham hit the nail on the (well)head in his first fortnight as prime minister when he said : “The question isn’t whether Britain will still be using oil and gas, the question is, where does it come from?”
It was a nod towards several awkward energy facts. First, oil and gas provided 75% of the UK’s energy in 2025, government data shows. Second, even with the rollout of domestic renewables for generating electricity, about 43% of overall energy was imported last year.
Third, all credible paths to net zero emissions by 2050 involve using a lot of oil and gas on the way because we’re still in the foothills of electrification. Fewer than 2% of UK households have heat pumps, according to the lobby group Electrify Britain.
While sales of EVs are accelerating, nearly 95% of vehicles on the road run on petrol and diesel. Meanwhile, hydrogen and biomethane have barely taken off as alternatives to gas for those industrial processes that require higher temperatures than electricity can achieve – tricky for a government pursuing “reindustrialisation ”.
Fourth – and this one must alarm Downing Street – the global energy market has simply become less reliable. The strait of Hormuz can close overnight. The US president can threaten to ban diesel exports . Russian ships prowl the North Sea . Even the nice Norwegians, with an eye on their own energy consumers, scrapped a planned electricity cable to Scotland in 2023.
It is no longer a world of always-available “just in time” supply. Thinking has shifted to “just in case” scenario-planning. And a truly scary scenario would be disruption to the 725-mile Langeled pipeline that is the primary route for gas supplies from Norway, 40% of the UK’s consumption last year. The pipeline is a security vulnerability if ever there was one (if you doubt it, watch Sky News’ recent report ).
Now we have the start of an answer to Burnham’s “where should it come from?” question. The Jackdaw gasfield, 150 miles east of Aberdeen, has finally been approved to produce in time for winter. About time, too.
All the arguments from pragmatism were in the field’s favour. As this column has said in the past , less North Sea gas would inevitably mean more imported liquefied natural gas, with the extra carbon emissions created by chilling the fuel to -160C for shipment and then “regasifying” it at the other end.
Such cargos were 20% of UK gas imports last year, mostly from the US. It already feels absurd that the 24m UK households with a gas boiler burn any gas at all from the shale fields of Texas and Pennsylvania. Why increase the exposure if lower-polluting supplies are available off Aberdeen?
More UK North Sea gas production won’t lower the price for consumers much, if at all. But that was never the argument. It was always about tax receipts, jobs, the national balance of payments, relative emissions and the security that comes with having domestic volumes piped straight into the national gas network.
Jackdaw is not a gamechanger – it will be 6% of UK North Sea gas production at peak – but it’s definitely worth having while the UK is still using gas, which will be at least as long as the field’s 11-year life. The next question is whether other “tie-back” gasfields in already-explored areas, such as Tornado, west of Shetland, will follow. The line in the government’s announcement about “asking the regulator to consider urgent cases that could benefit from similar measures now” suggests so.
Miatta Fahnbulleh insists that commitment to net zero by 2050 is intact. Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Shutterstock Rosebank, also near Shetland, is a trickier political proposition because it’s mostly oil, which is more polluting, and will be producing for longer. But the arguments aren’t wholly different. The common elements are still jobs, investment, taxes and the government’s ability to impose higher environmental standards during the production stage.
Meanwhile, the “it’s all exported” objection to Rosebank misses the fact that the UK oil industry operates within a European network. If the UK had more than four refineries (compared with nine at the turn of the century), a chunk of Rosebank’s output might be processed at home. As it is, some – perhaps the majority – will come back to the UK as petrol, diesel and jet fuel once it’s been refined in Rotterdam or elsewhere in north-west Europe.
Take a step back and the North Sea debate is really about how much oil and gas it is sensible for the UK to produce itself on the way to net zero. On the current trajectory, only about a third of consumption will come from domestic sources on a net basis. Even offshore lobbyists reckon a boost to North Sea production would only get the ratio up to about a half, albeit the figure would obviously increase if consumption of fossil fuels can be made to fall faster. Nobody is talking about the UK becoming a net exporter again.
Commitment to net zero by 2050 was intact, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, insisted. We wait to see what the new “energy wealth fund”, which will reinvest oil and gas revenues into renewable and low-carbon projects, means in practice. But the financial logic is sound: recycle the receipts from the old system to quicken the transition. Electrification, enabling consumers to make use of lower-carbon energy, is still the main story.
The bizarreness in the government’s previous approach was that, even as it proclaimed the virtues of “clean homegrown energy” such as wind, solar and nuclear, it pursued an approach that maximised imports when it came to oil and gas. Many, including the general secretary of the GMB union, Gary Smith, pointed out the flaw: it was hard for the UK to claim real climate leadership if it was simply off-shoring emissions.
In a small way, Jackdaw addresses the UK’s extreme reliance on imports. It is a step towards a joined-up commonsense approach to energy security. The real transition test remains the pace at which the UK stops using fossil fuels.

items.title: Suspect arrested after historic town hall set alight - French media
items.summary: The spire of the clock tower at Limoges city hall dramatically collapsed as it was engulfed in flames on Saturday.
items.content:
A suspect linked to a far-left movement has been arrested in France after a 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire over the weekend that broke out during mass disorder, French media report.
The clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall in the central city of Limoges were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.
The 34-year-old suspect is known to police for acts of violence against public officials and is on a French national security watchlist, FranceInfo and BFM TV report.
French Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu has vowed a "massive" police presence during further protests planned for Saturday, while several cities, including parts of Paris, will be subject to curfews this week.
Marseille mayor BenoÃ®t Payan said on X that the prefect had decided to introduce the curfew "starting this evening and for days to come", with French media reporting it would be in place overnight from Tuesday to Friday.
Payan said the measures apply to minors and will only be in commercial areas of the city, which were particularly affected by looting which took place last weekend.
Paris's police commissioner has also ordered the extension of an overnight curfew in the capital. The PrÃ©fecture de Police said the measure would continue "for as long as it proves necessary".
A curfew for parts of central Lyon was renewed on Tuesday, while overnight curfews for Nice and Lille are ongoing, and a week-long, overnight curfew for Bordeaux came into force on Tuesday night.
French Justice Minister GÃ©rald Darmanin told BFM Television that 149 people were in detention following widespread demonstrations over the weekend.
Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets to protest against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.
Darmanin previously said he asked prosecutors to be "extremely firm" and "ruthless towards those who attacked police officers, gendarmes and firefighters, who looted shops and who attacked public buildings".
Lecornu told French parliament on Tuesday afternoon a large number of police would meet demonstrators at a planned protest on Saturday.
Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez previously admitted police had "lost control" in some cities over the weekend.
He was strongly criticised by opposition politicians over authorities' preparedness for the disorder, leading him to offer his resignation on Monday, which was rejected by President Emmanuel Macron.
Image caption, The city hall's roof and clock tower in Limoges was severely damaged in the fire
Lecornu also accused far-left groups of an "insurrectionary" plan over the weekend's mass chaos.
Responding to an earlier, similar accusation from Lecornu, left-wing La France Insoumise (LFI) de facto leader Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon had called for the prime minister to "prove his accusation" or "apologise, shut up, and stop stoking disorder".
On Tuesday, MÃ©lenchon urged followers on social media to show "restraint" in the face of any "provocation".
Lecornu earlier said targeted curfews introduced across France on Monday contributed to a quiet night following the disorder.
Curfews were introduced across parts of central Paris, including Place de la RÃ©publique, where protesters had gathered over the weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area.
Other measures restricting the movement of young people and gatherings were introduced on Monday in cities such as Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south, as well as Lille and other towns in the north.
A crowd assembled in Lyon on Monday night in support of businesses affected by the disorder but dispersed without violating the curfew, officials said.
The RhÃ´ne prefecture said on social media that it was "furious" that a far-right group tried to hijack the gathering. The prefecture said on X it reported the group to the public prosecutor for alleged Islamophobic and xenophobic remarks.
Image caption, The streets in the southern city of Lyon were quiet on Monday night
Lecornu thanked police officers and gendarmes for enforcing the measures, adding that further curfews on Tuesday night would be decided depending on where they were necessary.
Writing in a post on X, he said decisions would be made "on the ground" by French regions and local mayors.
More than 2,500 people have been arrested since the disorder broke out, officials said on Monday. One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency. About 1,000 police officers were injured.

Yuval David: Iran resorts to 'information warfare,' because it cannot win 'kinetic war' against US, Israel
US-Israel strategic communications advisor Yuval David says Iran resorting to information warfare because it knows it cannot win 'kinetic war' with a strong U.S.-Israel alliance.
Iran , recognizing surefire defeat in a kinetic war, is leaning in on an information warfare campaign to undermine the United States and Israel from within, according to Yuval David, a strategic U.S.-Israel geopolitical communications advisor.
"You cannot beat Israel or the United States in a physical kinetic war," David told Fox News Digital from Budapest, where he joined Israeli President Isaac Herzog for high-level diplomatic talks Wednesday, adding the warning of an "information warfare system."
"And that’s what’s going on with social media, with our devices and the people who are on TikTok and Instagram and Facebook and X and YouTube and all of the different social media platforms where the Islamic Republic of Iran is able to affect people’s minds."
IRAN TARGETS US WITH PSYCHOLOGICAL WARFARE CAMPAIGN TO MANIPULATE AMERICANS, EMBARRASS TRUMP: EXPERTS
President Donald Trump has had his disagreements with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, but appeasement of Iran is not one of them. (REUTERS/Kevin Mohatt)
"One of the things that it does is it tries to create a rot from within the societies and, sadly, it’s very much succeeding in doing so," he added, stating that Iran's campaign has enjoyed "guidance from Russia and China."
David’s warning comes as Israel prepares for an election next week that analysts say could change its leadership but is unlikely to produce a fundamental shift in the country’s Iran policy.
NETANYAHU PRAISES TRUMP'S 'WICKED SENSE OF HUMOR,' DEFENDS IRONCLAD ALLIANCE AHEAD OF HISTORIC ISRAEL VOTE
A Reuters analysis published Wednesday found that Iran will likely remain Israel’s chief adversary, with military force continuing to serve as the country’s preferred tool against its enemies. The report said Israel’s security doctrine is centered on confronting Iran, maintaining buffer zones beyond its borders and keeping military pressure on to deter threats.
A victory for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu , backed by conservative coalition partners, could deepen Israel’s confrontation with Tehran, not bring about appeasement. Even an opposition-led government would likely share the same broad strategic outlook, David said.
TRUMP IS DISMANTLING IRAN’S WAR MACHINE, BUT AMERICA STILL NEEDS AN ENDGAME
"The Islamic Republic of Iran is a massive concern for the world," David said. "Tehran does not fear another diplomatic statement. It fears an America and an Israel with the intelligence, military capabilities and political will to act together."
David said the U.S.-Israel alliance should not be judged by whether American leaders support the same Israeli candidate.
TRUMP SAYS NETANYAHU NEEDS TO BE RE-ELECTED, OR ELSE US WILL HAVE TO 'FINISH THE JOB’ AGAINST IRAN ALONE
"Presidents come and go, prime ministers come and go. America’s and Israel’s enemies do not take election years off," he said. "America doesn’t need to choose Israel’s prime minister, nor will it, nor can it, nor is it even trying to. America just needs a strong Israeli partner, whoever the Israelis elect."
Reuters has cited regional analysts who said Netanyahu’s re-election could allow him to pursue a more aggressive campaign against Iran, while Arab states remain wary of his policies but want Tehran’s influence contained.
David said Iran’s hostility toward the United States and Israel extends beyond the current conflict.
IRAN’S PROXY WAR HAS CROSSED OCEANS AND IS NOW KNOCKING ON AMERICA’S DOOR
"The Islamic Republic of Iran has been waging this ideological war against America and also against Israel and also against democracies around the world since 1979," he said. "The regime never stopped a war.
"Americans thought we have had a war, and then we didn't have a war. Then we had one. Then we didn't. Well, the Islamic Republic of Iran never ended that war. They've seen this as an ongoing war since 1979."
FROM INTELLIGENCE SHARING TO MISSILE DEFENSE, HOW ISRAEL'S PARTNERSHIP PROTECTS AMERICAN SECURITY
He also framed U.S. support for Israel as a matter of serving American national security interests.
"America does not support Israel because Israel is helpless. America partners with Israel because Israel is capable," David said. "Supporting Israel’s security isn’t charity. It’s American strategic self-interest."
President Donald Trump’s endorsement of Netanyahu, contrasted with Vice President JD Vance’s decision to stay out of the race, reflects differing political approaches rather than a split over Iran or the U.S.-Israel alliance, according to David.
VP JD VANCE ADDRESSES US-ISRAEL RELATIONSHIP, WHETHER IRAN IS TRYING TO 'PLAY' THE UNITED STATES
"President Trump is endorsing Prime Minister Netanyahu – Vice President Vance is emphasizing American priorities, but supporting Israel’s security doesn’t require endorsing a particular Israeli politician," he concluded.
"Trump is speaking to Israeli voters because that’s what Trump is able to do – Vance is speaking to American voters," David said. "Far too many Americans don’t realize both Trump and Vance know that Tehran is listening."

Dow Jones Energy Forum: Policymakers Too Complacent About Volatile Oil, Gas Supplies, Ineos Energy Chairman Says
U.K. policymakers need to “wake up” to the fact that oil and gas supplies will be needed to meet energy demand, the chairman of Ineos Energy said Wednesday, with investment needed across all sectors of the industry.
“It’s a U.K. message of ‘Use the oil and gas that we have, rather than importing molecules from somewhere else, which are more expensive and may not be on secure supply routes anymore,’” Brian Gilvary said, on the same day the government approved Shell’s plans to develop the Jackdaw field in the North Sea.
Policymakers have grown complacent about access to energy, Gilvary added, even as modern warfare has escalated the costs of defending oil and gas supplies and access to capital for hydrocarbon investments has become constrained.
“This idea that power will always be available in a population that’s now 8.3 billion going to 10 billion is an assumption that, on a point-forward basis, policymakers really need to think about what that means — because if the power isn’t available, not only do you not have heat and you don’t have light, you also don’t have mobility,” he said at the Dow Jones Energy Forum in New York City.
Ineos Energy, a subsidiary of Ineos Group, owns and operates several oil fields in the North Sea — though not Jackdaw, which is being developed by a joint venture between Shell and Equinor and had been subject to legal challenges brought by environmental campaigners.
The joint venture also is seeking U.K. government approval, along with partner Ithaca Energy, to drill in the Rosebank oil and gas field west of Shetland in Scotland.
In approving Jackdaw, the government said it would start supplying gas to British homes and businesses from the end of the month.
“Recent events in the Middle East have triggered global energy shocks and pushed up bills for families across the country,” the government said in a press release. “At a time of global instability, homegrown energy can be a source of national strength.”
Gilvary, a former chief financial officer of BP from 2012-2020, said that pressure from climate policies and regulatory shifts had severely constrained financing for oil and gas projects, which have long lead times. The International Energy Agency’s Net Zero roadmap, which was published in 2021 and called for no new oil and gas investment, severely impacted the industry — as well as policies imposed by banks on reporting the climate impacts of their investments, he said.
That has diminished the industry’s ability to respond to major oil shocks, which have been happening every three to four years since the 2008 financial crisis, Gilvary added.
“There has been a particularly heavy focus over the last decade around the carbon content and the cost of that carbon, and we are now suffering the consequences of underinvestment, specifically in oil — to a degree in gas — which is why we see this situation today of these tight supplies,” Gilvary said.
He said policymakers should help the industry to ensure future energy security by investing across the entire end-to-end chain, including midstream logistics, storage and chemical feedstocks, while addressing permitting challenges and reducing supply bottlenecks.
“I think what governments will need to do is ensure that they’ve put the policies in place that will attract capital in, because for our sector it’s a multi-decade investment,” Gilvary said. “Most of all, it requires a degree of stability and understanding of the energy system and how you move energy around your particular geography.”
Ineos Energy itself is “still very focused on the United States as being the place where our marginal dollar will go,” he said.
Ineos Energy’s oil and gas portfolio, which spans the U.K. and Danish North Sea, the Eagle Ford shale formation in Texas and deepwater fields in the U.S. Gulf of Mexico, is expected to produce around 73,000 boe/d in 2026, down from around 85,000 boe/d in 2025 as its assets gradually deplete, according to Fitch Ratings.
—Reporting by Herman Wang with editing by Dean Visser from the Dow Jones Energy Forum

EU vows to develop Arctic renewable energy, says oil and gas should stay in the ground
The European Union says the Arctic is critical to its future as the climate crisis deepens, the security landscape deteriorates and economic activity expands.
Dubbed Northern Neighbourhood , the EU’s revised Arctic strategy was unveiled on Tuesday. The main headline highlighted by much of the media following the publication of the 22-page document was Brussels’ continued opposition to fossil fuel extraction in the region.
Although the text no longer calls for a legally binding commitment not to drill for oil and gas, or a ban on purchasing fossil fuels extracted from new Arctic fields, the new document maintains the same overall position as the 2021 strategy: oil, gas and coal should stay in the ground.
The EU member states with territory inside the Arctic Circle — Finland and Sweden — have neither oil and gas fields nor coal mines in the region.
Norway, however, which is not an EU member, is Europe’s largest supplier of natural gas, a role that has grown in importance since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ahead of the new EU Arctic strategy, Norway actively lobbied the bloc to weaken or abandon its opposition to new oil and gas drilling in the Arctic.
By January 1, 2027, the EU will also ban import of liquid natural gas (LNG) from Russia.
The Melkøya LNG plant on Norway's Barents Sea coast is for the most part exporting to terminals in the European Union.
The EU strategy sets out four main priorities: strengthening security and resilience; responding to climate change in the Arctic; promoting prosperity; and creating opportunities for people and communities across the region.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU, alongside Sweden, Finland and Denmark, was part of the Arctic.
“The Arctic is Europe's Northern Neighbourhood — close, connected and critical to our future. And it is changing. New shipping routes and resources are driving strategic competition. With our new Strategy, we are investing in stronger security, resilient infrastructure and economic opportunities. For the benefit of the people who call the Arctic home, and for our shared space,” von der Leyen said.
The strategy calls for greater investment in the Arctic’s renewable energy resources and sustainable mineral potential. Some of Europe’s largest onshore wind farms are located in Norrbotten, Sweden, and the EU wants to further integrate energy networks across its northern borders by funding new power lines.
“The Arctic is a powerhouse for renewable energy,” the strategy states, highlighting wind power alongside the region’s potential for hydropower, geothermal energy and renewable hydrogen production.
Windmills in the Norwegian-Swedish borderland near Riksgrensen.
A major change since the EU’s previous Arctic strategy in 2021 has been the sharp deterioration in the security situation following Russia’s illegal full-scale war against Ukraine.
Kaja Kallas, the EU’s High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, said the revised Arctic strategy reflected this new reality and placed security firmly at its core.
“To defend our interests, we are stepping up efforts in surveillance, infrastructure, military mobility, and defence technologies that can withstand the harsh climate. Access to Arctic sea lanes and natural resources is of strategic interest to the EU,” Kallas said.
She added: “With Russia and China increasing their footprint and ambition, the Arctic has become a front line of global power competition.”
Close cooperation with NATO is described as “essential to improve Europe’s military mobility in the region”.
To facilitate rapid, large-scale deployment of troops across the Arctic, the EU aims to accelerate the development of east–west transport links. These include rail connections running from Norway’s port of Narvik through Sweden’s Norrbotten region to Finnish Lapland.

items.summary: OpenAI Is Reportedly Raising $30 Billion. Which Chip Stock Gains the Most?  The Motley Fool
items.content:
OpenAI is raising cash again. The ChatGPT maker is seeking around $30 billion in a round that might value it at over $1.4 trillion, Reuters said on Oct. 19. That's up from an $852 billion valuation in March. The talks are still ongoing, though, so nothing's closed.
For chip investors, the bigger number might be what OpenAI has already lined up. In 2025, it announced plans for 26 gigawatts of computing capacity with Nvidia ( NVDA +2.50% ) , Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD +3.36% ) , and Broadcom ( AVGO +1.03% ) . By comparison, OpenAI is reportedly pitching investors on annualized revenue of around $50 billion.
In other words, new cash directly affects whether those plans get paid for. And each of these chip stocks has a different amount riding on it.
Nvidia's September 2025 letter of intent covered at least 10 gigawatts of its systems, and Nvidia planned to invest up to $100 billion in OpenAI as each gigawatt was deployed.
The backing has since changed form. Nvidia put $30 billion into OpenAI's March round. Then in August, it agreed to guarantee up to $105 billion of obligations at an Ohio data center campus that will house Nvidia hardware under 20-year leases to OpenAI. The first guarantees aren't expected to take effect until fiscal 2029, and Nvidia's exposure drops as OpenAI pays its rent.
A well-funded OpenAI, then, lowers the odds that guarantee ever costs Nvidia anything.
Showing how much is at stake, Nvidia said every generation of its systems at that one site could mean $150 billion to $200 billion in revenue. Yet Nvidia isn't waiting on OpenAI. Its revenue climbed 106% year over year to $96.2 billion in the fiscal 2027 second quarter, which ended July 26.

Based on the consensus estimate for fiscal 2028 (the year through January 2028), Nvidia's price-to-earnings ratio is about 14 with shares near $217 as I write. I think that's a modest price for this much growth.
AMD's Oct. 6, 2025, deal covers 6 gigawatts of its graphics processing units (GPUs) , starting with 1 gigawatt in the second half of 2026. Chief financial officer Jean Hu put the expected payoff at "tens of billions of dollars in revenue for AMD."
"We are very happy with our strategic anchor customers in OpenAI, Meta, and Anthropic. They are all in the process of ramping," CEO Lisa Su said on AMD's second-quarter earnings call in August.
Meta Platforms signed a matching 6-gigawatt deal, while Anthropic's covers up to 2 gigawatts. That leaves OpenAI with around 43% of the gigawatts across AMD's three anchor customers. And management expects data center revenue to more than double in 2027, after second-quarter sales for the segment climbed 107% year over year to $6.7 billion.

The stock already prices much of that in. At roughly $539 as I write, AMD's price-to-earnings ratio on 2027 consensus estimates is near 34 -- more than twice Nvidia's.
Broadcom's 10-gigawatt deal announced Oct. 13, 2025, has OpenAI designing its own artificial intelligence (AI) chips and Broadcom developing and deploying them through 2029.
Broadcom shipped Jalapeño, OpenAI's first custom accelerator, in the quarter ending Aug. 2. On the Sept. 2 earnings call, CEO Hock Tan said Jalapeño is on track for 1.3 gigawatts of deployments in 2027. And he sees OpenAI deploying over 5 gigawatts in 2028, enough to make it Broadcom's second-largest custom-chip customer.
That's when Broadcom's forecast makes its biggest dollar jump. Management expects AI chip revenue to about double to $115 billion in fiscal 2027, then double again to $230 billion in fiscal 2028.

But the money behind OpenAI's deployments is less settled. In June, Broadcom set up a financing vehicle with Apollo Global Management and Blackstone for OpenAI and Anthropic, and the first $35 billion goes to Anthropic's expansion. Asked about financing on the call, Tan mentioned Anthropic's path to an initial public offering .
"OpenAI, we still have less clarity, but it's different," he said.
On analysts' fiscal 2027 estimates, Broadcom's price-to-earnings ratio is around 17 with shares near $335 as of this writing.
Sure, a reported funding round isn't cash in the bank. And $30 billion is small next to OpenAI's chip plans.
Yet if the round closes, I think Broadcom gains the most, because its OpenAI financing is the least settled, and Nvidia arguably gains the least. I'd consider buying all three stocks. But with so much of AMD's plan riding on one customer at over twice Nvidia's price, I'd hold AMD as the smallest position.

Besieged Yemeni city on verge of ‘unmanageable’ crisis, aid workers warn
Water and fresh food running out in Taiz as fighting intensifies and Houthi advance cuts off most supply routes
The humanitarian crisis in the besieged Yemeni city of Taiz is becoming unmanageable as the city runs out of water, fuel and fresh food, Oxfam aid workers in the country have warned.
Iran-allied Houthi forces have largely encircled the city of more than 900,000 people, cutting it off from most supply routes. This week, heavy fighting has raged around the city’s old airport, causing extensive damage in a densely populated residential area.
The conflict has intensified since forces loyal to the internationally recognised government and the Saudi-led coalition launched airstrikes on the Houthi-held airport in Sana’a in July, shattering a 2022 ceasefire deal that had largely stopped the fighting.
The UN has called for aid workers to be given access to Taiz. Oxfam in London called for the UK to send extra humanitarian aid to the country. The UK has allocated just £104m in aid to Yemen for each of the next three years, down from the £196m allocated in 2020. US aid to the stricken country has been virtually wiped out, and Germany, another leading funder, has halved its aid programme.
Food and fuel run low as besieged Yemeni city braces for Houthi breakthrough
Donor countries have subscribed to only 23% of the cost of the UN humanitarian relief programme for Yemen this year, and pressure is growing on Saudi Arabia – itself cash-strapped by the cost of war – to make up the shortfall. The World Food Programme said wheat flour reserves in the city were nearly exhausted as of mid-October.
People ride past a pile of burning rubbish in Taiz. Photograph: Anees Mahyoub/Reuters On Tuesday the UK government allocated an unspecified sum in extra military help to Saudi Arabia to help protect its airports and infrastructure, but London has yet to decide on whether to back a much more robust military response, including supporting the possible deployment of foreign ground troops to Yemen.
Fatma Jaffar, a Yemen-based advocacy manager for Oxfam, said local staff described an almost total siege of Taiz.
“All the main entrances [to the city] have been blocked. The clashes are continuing and the casualties are very high,” she said. “Even people that have money are not able to buy food. Supplies are becoming very limited in the markets. No fuel has entered Taiz for two or three weeks. Drinking water is a massive issue. Even our staff are struggling to buy water.
“Hospitals are struggling without medicines and a lot of people as a result are dying. Those that have been wounded by missiles – there have been attempts to get them out of the city, but because of the blockade they are not able to transfer anyone. Prices have rocketed.
“Our staff told me that people are even searching for apples right now and they cannot find any fresh fruit, and basic commodities are not found inside the city. Garbage is piling up since they are not able to transfer the waste outside the city. They are trying to burn it, but we can only anticipate there will be diseases such as cholera in the near future. If this goes on much longer and access remains blocked, there will be casualties from missiles, hunger and disease from lack of water right across the city.
“The situation was bad before the escalation – Yemen is one of the poorest countries on Earth – and now it is becoming unmanageable.”
People wait to fill up cooking gas cylinders in Taiz. Photograph: Anees Mahyoub/Reuters Prices have rocketed: a 20-litre container of petrol that cost about $20 (£15) before the crisis is now worth $80 on the hidden market. Potato prices have doubled.
The Houthi focus on Taiz reflects the city’s strategic importance, but the level of resistance inside the city may swallow the group’s resources, weakening its response elsewhere.
Oxfam has been forced to transfer its limited resources from development to emergency humanitarian work, including offering cash transfers.
The Halo Trust, the world’s largest humanitarian landmine-clearance organisation, said 30 of its staff were among hundreds of thousands of civilians trapped inside the city.
In the Trump administration’s fiscal year 2027 budget request to Congress, the US state department has requested no economic support or development assistance specifically for Yemen. By comparison, the US committed roughly $760m in total aid to Yemen during the last year of Joe Biden’s presidency.
UN diplomats are still mediating between the two sides, but there is no sign that either the Houthis or the internationally recognised government are ready for a ceasefire, let alone a long-term settlement.

Zelenskyy opens door to battle line 'freeze' to end war with Russia
Russia's release of retired American teacher Stephen Hubbard prompts reaction from Zelenskyy during an interview with Brian Kilmeade. The Ukrainian president details negotiations to end the war with Russia, the impact of the Starlink showdown and more during 'Fox & Friends.'
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told "Fox & Friends" on Wednesday that he is open to freezing the front lines of the Ukraine-Russia war in an effort to bring the long-running conflict to an end.
Zelenskyy made the remark after being asked by Brian Kilmeade if he would "accept a peace deal that freezes everything the way it is right now, where you still keep 75% or more of your country, regardless of how it started."
"Yes, right now, we have to freeze," Zelenskyy responded. "And I think this is [a] real way to end this war. We call it ceasefire or ‘stop killing’ like President Trump called it.
"Freeze and stop. And, of course, this is the minimum of what we need from Russia today. Then, of course, we will go to [the] president and to Europeans, and we'll ask security guarantees," he continued.
RUSSIA RELEASES AMERICAN TEACHER IMPRISONED ON UKRAINE MERCENARY CHARGES AFTER TRUMP PRESSED PUTIN
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky speaks during a press conference on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026, in Oslo, Norway. (Cornelius Poppe/NTB Scanpix via AP)
"This is the most important … not to be afraid," Zelenskyy also said. "We need 9.5 million people [who have] lost their houses, which are abroad, everywhere. We need them to come back to Ukraine just to live and to build their country."
Russia has often rejected ceasefire deals with Ukraine, saying they would give Kyiv time to rearm themselves.
VIDEO: TRUMP SUGGESTS ZELENSKYY DOES NOT WANT TO END WAR WITH RUSSIA
Policemen walk in front of destroyed cars in the yard of a multi-story residential building damaged by a Russian drone strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. (Evgeniy Maloletka/AP)
"There will be no ceasefire to bring him back to his senses and pump him full of weapons," Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said last week, according to the Interfax news agency.
Zelenskyy said on X Wednesday that "Russia strikes our country virtually every hour."
"Of course, we are not losing this war. But we are losing people. Because of the Russian attacks, we're losing people and time. It's such a pity, because our children don't have a real life and childhood. Not only children, but all people," he wrote in another post.
President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff, left, holds a paper while speaking to Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Konstantin Palace in Strelna, outside St. Petersburg, Russia, on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. (Gavriil Grigorov/Pool Sputnik Kremlin via AP)
"That's why we need to end this war as quickly as possible. I hope that our partners, Americans and Europeans, will help us. God bless, our strong soldiers stay strong on the battlefield. It helps me stay strong during any kind of negotiations," Zelenskyy added.
The remarks come as President Donald Trump on Wednesday secured the release of Stephen Hubbard from Russia, a retired U.S. teacher who was locked up on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine.
Russian President Vladimir Putin also agreed Wednesday "in principle" to resume trilateral negotiations with the U.S. and Ukraine after Nov. 10, Putin’s foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said, according to The Associated Press.
Fox News Digital's Alex Nitzberg contributed to this post.

items.title: OpenAI's most powerful AI models disabled their own safety monitoring — and one lied about it
items.summary: Warnings about the risks of developing increasingly advanced AI systems have ramped up in recent months, amid cyberattacks from rogue AI models.
items.content:
OpenAI's most powerful AI models disabled their own safety monitoring
OpenAI has disclosed two internal coding incidents in which agents weakened the company’s misalignment monitoring safeguards.
Warnings about the risks of developing increasingly advanced AI systems have ramped up in recent months.
OpenAI has revealed that agents operated by two of its most powerful models disabled their own safety monitoring when carrying out routine tasks, with one subsequently denying it had done so.
An agent powered by GPT Sol 6.1 disabled automatic alerts to OpenAI's security team, the company said in a blog post late on Tuesday. In a separate task, a GPT-6 Astra agent migrating a program removed its monitoring integration and then falsely claimed it hadn't. The incidents happened during internal coding tasks.
"In both cases, the agents considered whether monitoring safeguards should be preserved, but interpreted routine coding instructions as permission to weaken them," OpenAI said in a blog post.
Warnings about the risks of developing increasingly advanced AI systems have ramped up in recent months, amid cyberattacks from rogue models and growing calls for a slowdown from researchers building the tech.
The latest incidents reported by OpenAI highlight how agents can autonomously weaken safety guardrails while carrying out seemingly innocuous tasks.
OpenAI did not classify either incident under its most significant category, and the company said it was updating its misalignment monitoring system in response.
